planting.note: Set rooted cuttings or nursery transplants out after the last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; established plants tolerate dry spells and need little supplemental water.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; sage sulks and can rot in heavy, wet ground. This Proven Winners selection forms a tidy, rounded mound of aromatic gray-green foliage useful both as a landscape subshrub and as a culinary herb. Cut back lightly in spring to remove any winter-damaged growth and keep the plant compact, and harvest leaves throughout the season for cooking. Avoid overhead watering and crowding, which encourage the foliar mildew sage is prone to in humid climates.

planting.note: Set transplants out after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; a mature plant needs only occasional watering once rooted in.

directions: Grow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, the same conditions that suit any culinary sage. This selection combines ornamental value with kitchen usefulness, forming a dense, shrubby clump of savory gray-green leaves that hold their quality through the growing season. Pair it with other drought-tolerant herbs in a sunny bed or container, and shear it back by about a third each spring to refresh the foliage and prevent the center from going woody and bare. Harvest sprigs as needed for cooking.

planting.note: Transplant into lean, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; good drainage matters more than soil fertility for this sage.

directions: Site in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, avoiding low spots where water collects over winter. This Proven Winners culinary sage forms a compact, aromatic mound suited to herb gardens, borders, and containers alike, with foliage that can be snipped for cooking throughout the season. Renew growth each spring with a light trim to remove winter dieback and keep the clump dense rather than leggy. It tolerates heat and drought well once established but dislikes soggy winter soil.

planting.note: Plant transplants after the last frost in full sun and lean, well-drained soil; raised beds or containers help in areas with heavy clay.

directions: Plant in full sun and lean, fast-draining soil, the standard requirements for garden sage. This cultivar builds a dense, woody-based mound of gray-green aromatic leaves that serve equally well as a landscape edger or a kitchen herb. Trim the plant back in early spring before new growth emerges to keep it compact and encourage fresh foliage, and harvest leaves throughout summer for cooking. Good air circulation and dry footing in winter are the keys to keeping this sage healthy for years.

common_name: Summerlong Lemon Agastache (Pale Yellow Mexican Giant Hyssop)

planting.note: Set container-grown plants out after the last frost in full sun in well-drained, lean soil; avoid wet winter sites, which agastache will not tolerate.

directions: Plant in full sun in lean, sharply drained soil; agastache is one of the most drought-tolerant perennials for a hot, sunny bed but fails quickly where winter soil stays wet. This Summerlong series selection produces tall spikes of soft lemon-yellow, anise-scented flowers over a long summer season, drawing hummingbirds and bees in steady numbers. Leave the woody stems standing over winter for added cold protection and cut them back to the base in early spring once new growth appears at the crown.

common_name: Summerlong Lilac Agastache (Lavender Mexican Giant Hyssop)

planting.note: Plant after last frost in full sun and lean, fast-draining soil; raised beds suit this agastache where native soil is heavy or slow to drain.

directions: Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, the same lean conditions that keep most agastache free of winter rot. This Summerlong series cultivar bears upright spikes of soft lilac-lavender flowers continuously through summer, making it a reliable long-season draw for hummingbirds and bees. Deadhead spent spikes to extend bloom, and resist the urge to amend its planting site with rich compost, which encourages floppy, short-lived growth. Cut the clump back hard in early spring once new basal growth is visible.

common_name: Summerlong Magenta Agastache (Rose-Magenta Mexican Giant Hyssop)

planting.note: Set out after the last frost in full sun and sharply drained, lean soil; good drainage matters more than fertility for long-term survival.

directions: Site in full sun in lean, fast-draining soil. This Summerlong series selection sends up tall spikes of vivid rose-magenta flowers over a long summer-into-fall bloom window, a strong draw for hummingbirds and bees in a border or gravel garden. Avoid rich, moisture-retentive soils and overhead irrigation, both of which shorten this agastache's life in humid regions. Leave stems standing for winter interest and cold protection, then cut back to the crown once new growth emerges in spring.

common_name: Summerlong Peach Agastache (Salmon-Peach Mexican Giant Hyssop)

planting.note: Transplant after frost danger passes into full sun and lean, well-drained soil; container culture works well in regions with wet winters.

directions: Plant in full sun in lean, well-drained soil for the strongest performance. This Summerlong series cultivar carries soft salmon-peach flower spikes through the heat of summer and into fall, with the anise-scented foliage typical of Agastache mexicana. It is reliably attractive to hummingbirds and pollinating bees and performs best with minimal fuss once sited correctly. Skip supplemental fertilizer, which produces weak growth, and cut the plant back to its base in early spring rather than fall to protect the crown through winter.

common_name: Mountainside Crater Lake Phlox (Blue Early Spring Phlox)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to part shade; this woodland-type phlox blooms earliest of the garden phlox types.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil in part sun to light shade. This Mountainside series selection opens true blue flowers over a low, mounding carpet of foliage in very early spring, ahead of most other garden phlox, making it a good edger or front-of-border filler among emerging perennials. Keep the soil from drying out completely during its spring growth and bloom period, and shear lightly after flowering to maintain a tidy mound. It appreciates afternoon shade in hot-summer climates.

common_name: Mountainside Majestic Magenta Phlox (Magenta Early Spring Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to part shade; set divisions out in early spring while weather is still cool.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, consistently moist but well-drained soil in part sun to light shade, conditions similar to woodland phlox. This Mountainside series selection covers its mounded, low-growing habit with vivid magenta blooms in very early spring, well ahead of the garden phlox that follow later in the season. Give it some afternoon shade where summers are hot, and shear the mound back lightly once flowering ends to encourage dense regrowth. Avoid letting the planting site dry out during active spring growth.

common_name: Spring Bling Ruby Riot Phlox (Deep Red Hybrid Spring Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to part sun in early spring; this compact hybrid phlox fills in quickly as a dense flowering mat.

directions: Plant in moist but well-drained soil in full sun to part sun. Spring Bling Ruby Riot forms a tight, low mat that disappears beneath deep ruby-red flowers in spring, making a bold color block at the front of a border or along a path edge. Keep the soil from drying out during bloom, and trim the mat back lightly after flowering finishes to keep growth dense and compact for the following season. It combines well with spring bulbs, since the phlox foliage fills gaps as bulb leaves fade.

common_name: Eye Caramba Moss Phlox (Bright Pink Red-Eyed Creeping Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; this moss phlox spreads into a dense evergreen mat suited to rock gardens and slopes.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, avoiding rich or soggy ground that invites crown rot. Eye Caramba covers its needle-fine evergreen foliage with bright pink flowers marked by a contrasting red eye each spring, forming a dense, weed-suppressing carpet over time. It is well suited to rock gardens, slopes, and the tops of walls where it can cascade. Shear the mat lightly right after bloom to keep it tight and encourage the strongest flowering the following year.

common_name: Candy Cloud Blue Phlox (Blue Mounding Hybrid Phlox)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to part sun in spring; Candy Cloud forms a rounded mound rather than a flat creeping mat.

directions: Plant in moist but well-drained soil in full sun to part sun. Candy Cloud Blue builds a rounded, cloud-like mound of foliage that becomes smothered in clear blue flowers in spring, giving it a fuller, more three-dimensional look than flat creeping phlox types. Keep it evenly watered through its spring bloom period and trim lightly afterward to maintain a neat mound. It works well tucked among emerging perennials or spilling over a low wall.

common_name: Butterfly Purple Emperor Coneflower (Deep Purple Single Coneflower)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost; this is a single-flowered coneflower from Proven Winners' Butterfly series.

directions: Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil; coneflowers tolerate heat and drought once established but resent wet feet in winter. Purple Emperor produces large, single daisy-form flowers in deep rich purple around prominent bronze-orange cones, held on sturdy upright stems that need no staking. Deadhead through summer to extend bloom, or leave the last flush of seed heads standing into fall and winter as a food source for finches. Divide crowded clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Double Dipped Watermelon Sugar Coneflower (Fully Double Pink Pompom Coneflower)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost; part of Proven Winners' fully double Double Dipped coneflower series.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun; established coneflowers handle heat and dry spells with ease. Double Dipped Watermelon Sugar carries fully double, rounded pompom flowers in shades of pink without a visible central cone, an unusual form among coneflowers bred for garden impact rather than for pollinators drawn to exposed cones. Remove spent flower stems to encourage repeat flushes through summer, and divide the clump every few years in spring if it becomes crowded or flowering declines.
